title: grep Advanced & Practical Usage 🕵️
description: Apply regex with grep flags, extended regex mode, and real-world log parsing.

slides.title: Recap: grep Essentials 📜
slides.content:
## Flags We Love

- `-E` – extended regex (ERE) for richer patterns.
- `-i` – case‑insensitive.
- `-v` – invert match.
- `-r` / `-R` – recursive directory search.
- `-n` – line numbers.
- `-c` – count matches.
- `-l` – list filenames only.
- `-o` – show only the matched part, not whole line.
- `-w` – whole word match.

slides.title: Recursive Search & File Context 🗂️
slides.content:
## Grepping Whole Projects

`grep -r 'TODO' .` searches all files under current directory.
`grep -r --include='*.sh' 'FIXME'` limits to .sh files.
`grep -rl 'error' /var/log/` lists file paths containing "error" without showing the lines.

quizData.question: `grep -rl 'error' /var/log/` prints the actual lines containing 'error'.
quizData.explanation: `-l` lists only the filenames where matches were found, not the matching lines.

slides.title: Real‑World Log Parsing 🗄️
slides.content:
## Combine Everything

Scenario: Apache access log. Extract all IPs that accessed 'admin.php' and got a 200 status.

Sample log line: `192.168.1.1 - - [22/May/2026:10:00:00] "GET /admin.php HTTP/1.1" 200 1234`

Regex:
```bash
grep 'admin.php' access.log | grep '" 200 ' | awk '{print $1}'
```
Or purely with grep: `grep -Eo '^[^ ]+' access.log` for IPs.

slides.title: Regex in Conditionals 🧪
slides.content:
## Using `=~` in `[[ ]]`

Bash's `[[ ]]` supports regex with the `=~` operator:
```bash
if [[ "$email" =~ ^[a-z]+@[a-z]+\.[a-z]{2,}$ ]]; then
   echo "Valid"
fi
```
No need for `grep`; you can validate inside the script.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content: Build and test your regex with `echo 'test string' | grep -E 'PATTERN'` before embedding it in a script. Use `-n` for line numbers when scanning large files.
